text:
What a charm life has, if native winds

on their light wings bring lost echoes

of stream music and nest music,

like gentle preludes from soft instruments!


What a charm life has, if beneath the bohío's shelter,

amid an intense fragrance of lilies and basil,

we look at the corrals where the cows low

and hear the stanzas of the murmuring river!...


The soil is the source of inspiration:

why seek happiness in foreign lands,

if we have Decembers thick with stars,

if we have Octobers pregnant with illusions!


Not from the Pagan Mount does the inspiring muse descend

to the estates of pale poets:

our native muse lives in the arbors of purple and mother-of-pearl,

where dawn dies.


It is our Indian muse who, from her cabin,

descends crowned with quetzal feathers

to inspire simple, tender madrigals,

fragrant with forest and mountain flowers.


Come, then, let us dream beneath warm eaves

of flowering orange trees, beside the springs:

October gives us its roses and evening blooms;

December the myriads of all its stars.

translation.title: Let Us Sing Our Own
translation.editorial_note: The source’s “silos natales vientos” is read as the evident “si los natales vientos” (“if native winds”); the translation preserves the native muse and seasonal imagery.
